back: The longest path through the network. It determines the shortest possible project duration.
A method to estimate the minimum project duration and the float on each path, using a forward and a backward pass. It ignores resource limits.

front: Total float of a critical activity
back: Normally zero. Any delay to it delays the project.
Works from the project start to the end and calculates early start (ES) and early finish (EF).
Works from the project end to the start and calculates late finish (LF) and late start (LS).
EF = ES + duration − 1. With the day-0 convention: EF = ES + duration.
LS = LF − duration + 1. With the day-0 convention: LS = LF − duration.

front: Forward pass at a merge (several predecessors)
back: Take the LARGEST early finish of the predecessors.

front: Backward pass where an activity has several successors
back: Take the SMALLEST late start of the successors.
The time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project finish date. LS − ES, or LF − EF.
The time an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of its successor.
Total float protects the project end date. Free float protects the next activity.

front: Is total float owned by one activity?
back: No. Total float is shared along a path: if an earlier activity uses it, less is left for later ones. Free float belongs to an individual activity.
Occurs when an imposed date or constraint is earlier than logic and durations allow. The schedule cannot meet the date as planned.
A path with very little float. A small delay can turn it into a critical path.

front: Can a project have more than one critical path?
back: Yes. More critical paths means higher schedule risk.
Shortening the schedule duration without reducing the project scope. Two techniques: crashing and fast tracking.
Shortening the schedule for the least incremental cost by adding resources (overtime, more people, paying for faster delivery). Increases cost.
Performing in parallel activities that are normally done in sequence. Increases risk and may cause rework.
Only those on the critical path. Shortening a non-critical activity does not shorten the project.

front: Which critical activity to crash first?
back: The one with the least additional cost per unit of time saved.
Adjusts start and finish dates to resolve overallocated or limited resources. May change the critical path and delay the project.
Adjusts activities only within their free and total float. The critical path and finish date do not change.
The overall technique for generating the schedule model. It uses the critical path method, resource optimization and modeling techniques.
Evaluating scenarios to predict their effect on project objectives, such as the schedule.
The most common simulation technique. Runs the model many times with varying inputs to show the range and probability of possible outcomes.
A schedule method that places buffers on schedule paths to account for limited resources and project uncertainties.
Convergence: an activity with several predecessors. Divergence: an activity with several successors. Both are points of higher schedule risk.

front: Critical path activity vs critical activity
back: Critical path activity: on the critical path. Critical activity: vital to project success, usually high risk, even if it is not on the critical path.
The longest resource-leveled path through the schedule, including buffers. Often different from the critical path.
Critical chain: time added at the end of the project, between the last activity and the delivery date, to protect the end date.
Critical chain: time added where a chain of non-critical activities feeds into the critical chain.
Critical chain: an early warning placed along the critical chain that a resource will be needed. It adds no time to the project.
An activity lacking a predecessor, a successor or both. It creates a false appearance of float. Only the start and finish milestones may be open-ended.
